notable_claims: Swiss network provider SWITCH refused to carry newsgroups like alt.drugs and clari.news.terrorism based on potential illegality.
Iowa State University implemented a policy banning discussions of sex and drugs on Usenet.
Carnegie Mellon University allegedly used threats of sexual harassment investigations to discourage offensive public writing.
The 'alt' newsgroups were created to fight suppression rather than as a designated area for dangerous topics.
classification.summary: This abstract summarizes several incidents regarding censorship, privacy, and network administration in academic environments. Key examples include the banning of Usenet groups by Swiss universities and Iowa State University, as well as disputes over password-cracking software and student directory privacy.
classification.title: Article 0 -- Abstract of CAF-News 02.11

notable_claims: Switch implemented a four-category classification system for newsgroups, including 'Prohibited Newsgroups'.
The prohibited list included groups such as alt.politics.homosexuality and talk.politics.guns.
Brossard claims that Switch's censorship is based on moral bias rather than actual Swiss law, except possibly regarding pornography.
classification.summary: Alain Brossard of EPFL criticizes Switch, the federal institution linking Swiss universities, for implementing a newsgroup classification system that bans various Usenet groups. The banned list includes topics related to homosexuality, drugs, and politics, which Brossard argues exceeds legal requirements and constitutes censorship. He suggests alternative network feeds via CHUUG or direct international NNTP connections to bypass these restrictions.
classification.title: Censorship and bigotism come up strong in Switzerland

identity.subject: Article 1--Censorship and bigotism come up strong in Switzerland

notable_claims: The distribution of abortion information was illegal in Ireland under a strict interpretation of the Eighth Amendment.
There was concern that allowing crossposts from talk.abortion to be read on Irish servers could lead to legal prosecution for distributing prohibited information.
organizations: Society for the Protection of the Unborn Child
classification.summary: Paul Moloney discusses the legal restrictions on abortion information in Ireland and how these laws may apply to the internet. He questions whether hosting newsgroup posts containing clinic contact information constitutes illegal distribution of abortion services. The post highlights a tension between national censorship laws and the technical nature of network data transmission.
classification.title: The Irish Abortion Controversy

notable_claims: The actual ISU policy was created without user participation and over the objections of the Computer Advisor Committee.
Administrators used a redefined version of 'academic freedom' to justify banning newsgroups that might offend others.
The author claims the administration ignored federal district court decisions (Doe v. U. of Michigan and UWM Post v. U. of Wisconsin) regarding censorship at state universities.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie presents a parody of the official Usenet news policy at Iowa State University to criticize its censorship practices. The piece argues that the administration's restrictions on newsgroups were implemented without user input and ignored established case law regarding academic freedom. It highlights the tension between computer administrators' control over network content and the university's role as a marketplace of ideas.
classification.title: What if the Iowa State U. Usenet policy was honest?

identity.subject: Article 3--What if the Iowa State U. Usenet policy was honest?

notable_claims: The university's threat of investigation for continuing to bring complaints constitutes a 'chilling effect'.
Conditional forbearance by an institution can be viewed as harassment of the student.
Academic settings should not shield adults from offensive or brutish speech.
classification.summary: Howard Goldstein critiques Carnegie Mellon University's handling of a student's speech, arguing that the university's threat of investigation creates a 'chilling effect.' He contends that conditional forbearance by the administration acts as a form of harassment and censorship. Goldstein suggests that shielding students from offensive speech in an academic setting is ethically irresponsible.
classification.title: Article 4--Speech Restrictions On Cm

notable_claims: Possession of password-cracking software was treated as a violation of ethics/policy by university administration.
The user claims the software was held for research into computer security and shadow password systems.
organizations: The Indiana Academy for Science, Mathematics, and the Humanities
classification.summary: Bryan Strawser reports that his university's Unix system administrators implemented restrictive policies and warnings after discovering password-cracking software on several user accounts. Strawser argues that the mere possession of such tools for research purposes should not be equated with unethical behavior or a violation of policy. He describes a confrontation with his department chairman regarding his UNIX privileges.
classification.title: Article 5--(none)

notable_claims: Server operators can determine the exact interests of users by collecting natural language queries and accessed documents.
The lack of human contact in digital interactions may lead to a decay in respect for patron privacy compared to physical libraries.
Users may be less willing to explore new or 'ignorant' subjects if they feel their search history is being monitored.
classification.summary: Brewster Kahle discusses the ethical responsibilities of operators of electronic information servers, specifically using the Wide Area Information Server (WAIS) as an example. He argues that 'digital librarians' have access to sensitive user query data and must adopt a professional code of ethics similar to traditional reference librarians to protect user privacy. The piece warns that surveillance of search queries can stifle intellectual curiosity and learning.
classification.title: Ethics of Digital Librarianship

notable_claims: Questions whether computer accounts or email can be legally conditioned on the disclosure of a student's name and phone number.
Cites 34 C.F.R. 99.7(b) suggesting institutions may not require FERPA waivers as a condition for admission or services.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie questions whether a university can legally condition the provision of services, specifically computer accounts and email access, on a student's agreement to release directory information. The post cites FERPA regulations and legal compendiums regarding the definition of directory information and the illegality of requiring waivers as a condition for receiving benefits.
classification.title: Requiring students to release directory information

identity.subject: Article 7--Requiring students to release directory information

notable_claims: User accounts were disabled without prior warning or communication via available contact methods.
classification.summary: Mark Evans reports that his accounts at the University of Aston were disabled without prior notice due to alleged network congestion caused by a program he was running. He criticizes the system administrators for disabling access rather than communicating with the user first.
classification.title: Article 8--Sys-admins shooting first

notable_claims: The NSF typically avoids acting on Usenet discussions until a formal paper complaint is received.
Responsibility for unauthorized network use lies with the insecure remote system providing inadequate authentication, not the transit host (MIT).
Privatization of the network will likely eliminate open-access services like TERMINUS to enable traffic monitoring and billing.
classification.summary: The author discusses the controversy surrounding TERMINUS, a system providing open access to the network, and whether the NSF should regulate its use. Donelan argues that the responsibility for security lies with the destination systems rather than the transit provider (MIT). He suggests that privatization of the network will likely end such open-access services due to traffic control and billing needs.
classification.title: Article 9--Re: NSFnet rules of use and terminus

identity.subject: Article 9--Re: NSFnet rules of use and terminus

notable_claims: The 'alt' hierarchy was created to bypass the 'backbone cabal' of administrators who controlled news flow.
The group comp.women passed a vote but was refused by many system administrators who viewed it as non-technical and political.
Early Usenet governance involved a small number of influential academic sites that acted as a backbone.
Groups like alt.censorship and alt.acad-freedom exist in the 'alt' hierarchy because their creators viewed formal voting procedures as fascist.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the origins of the Usenet 'alt' hierarchy as a response to censorship by the 'backbone cabal'. The text describes how administrators at major academic and commercial sites refused to propagate certain groups, such as comp.women, despite successful votes. This led users to create an alternate hierarchy propagated via UUCP links to bypass centralized control.
classification.title: Article 10--Re: History of "alt" groups
